Vignette: Hemi

Hemi is a 55-year-old Māori man who works as a nanny for two young children in a well-to-do suburb. He is quiet in the way that some large men are — not unfriendly, but careful, as though he has learned to take up less space than his body suggests. He has been divorced for four years, lives alone in a small flat, and describes his work with the children as the thing that keeps him moving forward each morning. He says this without sentimentality. He means it literally.

Three years ago, Hemi's adult son, Rangi, was struck by a car while crossing an intersection near his university. Hemi received the call at work. He drove to the hospital, and what he found there — Rangi unconscious, his skull fractured, tubes running in and out of him like something mechanical — is an image Hemi cannot put down. He stood at the bedside for hours without sitting. He did not cry. He kept thinking that if he stayed very still, time might slow enough for him to figure out what to do. Rangi survived, but spent eight months in rehabilitation and still walks with a permanent limp and struggles with memory. Hemi watched all of it. He was there for every appointment, every setback, every moment when his son could not remember the word for something simple. He held himself together through all of it, and then, once Rangi was stable and living independently again, something in Hemi quietly came apart.

He began having nightmares almost immediately — not always about the accident itself, but about arriving too late, about finding an empty hospital bed, about Rangi as a child again, small and unreachable. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning and cannot return to sleep. During the day, he finds himself scanning for danger in ways he cannot fully control. When he is driving the children he cares for to school, he grips the steering wheel tightly at every intersection. He checks the mirrors constantly. He has begun taking longer routes to avoid the particular configuration of roads that reminds him of where Rangi was hit. The children have noticed he goes a different way now and have asked why. He told them the other road has too many bumps.

Hemi does not talk about any of this with the children's parents, who regard him as steady and dependable — which he is, at work. He is genuinely good with children. He is patient and warm and he reads to them in te reo Māori, which he is quietly proud of. But at the end of each day, when the house empties and he drives home alone, the careful composure he has maintained begins to dissolve. He often sits in his car in the car park outside his flat for twenty or thirty minutes before he can go inside. He does not know what he is waiting for.

He has largely withdrawn from his social world. He was once close with his brothers and attended regular kapa haka practice, but he stopped going about a year ago. He tells himself he is tired, which is true, but he also knows that being around people who knew him before — who knew Rangi before — requires a kind of performance he no longer has the energy for. His divorce, which preceded the accident, had already left him feeling unmoored. The accident deepened that feeling into something closer to a permanent condition.

What troubles Hemi most, he says, is not the nightmares or the exhaustion, but the sense that he is watching his own life from slightly outside of it. He loves Rangi. He is grateful his son is alive. But gratitude and grief, he has discovered, are not opposites. They sit in him at the same time, heavy and unresolved, and he is not sure anyone around him understands that both things can be true at once.
